subject: chemistry
title: Electron configuration and orbitals
key_idea: Electrons sit in shells, which are split into **sub-shells** (s, p, d), which are made of **orbitals**. Each orbital holds up to two electrons with opposite spins. Electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first, and fill orbitals of equal energy singly before pairing.

blocks.text: Electrons are arranged in levels of energy. This section covers shells, sub-shells and orbitals, and how many electrons each can hold.

items.meaning: A group of orbitals with the same principal quantum number, n. Shell 1 is closest to the nucleus and lowest in energy.
A group of orbitals of the same type within a shell: s, p or d.
A region around the nucleus that can hold up to two electrons, which must have opposite spins.

rows: Dumbbell, with two lobes. The three p orbitals point along the x, y and z axes.

items: Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons.
An s orbital is a sphere around the nucleus. A larger shell has a larger s orbital.
The p orbitals in one sub-shell all have the same energy.
An orbital holds two electrons at most, with opposite spins.
s has 1 orbital (2 electrons), p has 3 (6) and d has 5 (10).
The first four shells hold 2, 8, 18 and 32 electrons.
s orbitals are spherical and p orbitals are dumbbell shaped.

blocks.text: In an atom in its lowest energy state, called the ground state, electrons follow three rules.

items: Electrons fill the orbital of **lowest energy** first.
An orbital holds two electrons at most, and they have **opposite spins**.
Orbitals of the same energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, are filled **singly first**. Electrons pair up only when every orbital in the sub-shell has one electron.
Electrons repel each other, so they spread out into separate orbitals rather than sharing one.

blocks.text: The 4s sub-shell is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first. The full order is 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p.
Each orbital is drawn as a box and each electron as an arrow. Oxygen, with 8 electrons, shows the rule for singly before pairing.

Fill orbitals of equal energy singly before pairing.
Two electrons in one orbital have opposite spins, drawn as ↑↓.

blocks.text: A configuration lists each sub-shell with its number of electrons as a superscript. This section covers atoms and ions up to Z = 36.

items.text: For an atom, this is the atomic number. Chlorine has 17.
Fill each sub-shell to its maximum: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

items: **Shorthand:** write the previous noble gas in brackets, then the rest. Iron is [Ar] 3d⁶4s².
**Positive ions:** take electrons from the outer shell. Mg²⁺ has lost its two 3s electrons.
**Negative ions:** add electrons to the next free place. Cl⁻ has gained one electron in 3p.
**Chromium and copper are exceptions.** Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹, because a half-full or full 3d sub-shell is more stable.
Count the electrons first, then fill in order.
For a positive ion remove electrons. For a negative ion add them.
Cr and Cu are exceptions: each has one electron in 4s.

items: Filling is limited to the first three shells and the 4s and 4p orbitals.
Ions are limited to the s-block and p-block elements up to Z = 36.
Models for electron structure have been developed and refined as new evidence has appeared.

blocks.text: Ideas about electron configuration came from three kinds of evidence.

items: **Atomic emission spectra** show lines at fixed frequencies. Electrons can only have certain energies, so this is evidence for quantum shells.
**Successive ionisation energies** rise in steps. A big jump shows that the next electron is in a lower shell, which also shows the group of the element.
**First ionisation energies** of successive elements dip at certain points. Those dips are evidence for sub-shells.

blocks.text: Configurations are given in 1s notation and in electrons-in-boxes notation. Ions are limited to the s-block and p-block up to Z = 36.

items: Emission spectra: evidence for quantum shells.
Successive ionisation energies: evidence for shells and the group.
First ionisation energies across elements: evidence for sub-shells.

blocks.text: This course also asks how ionisation energies give evidence for shells and sub-shells. The next note covers it in full.

items: Define first ionisation energy and write equations for first and successive ionisation energies.
Successive ionisation energies jump when electrons start to come from a lower shell, which is evidence for shells.
First ionisation energies across Period 3 and down Group 2 dip and rise in ways that are evidence for sub-shells.
Big jumps in successive ionisation energies are evidence for shells.
Dips in first ionisation energy are evidence for sub-shells.

items.meaning: The number of the shell: n = 1, 2, 3 and so on. A higher n means higher energy and a greater distance from the nucleus.
The arrangement of electrons with the lowest total energy.

items: Give the number of electrons in each shell, sub-shell and orbital. Iron is 2, 8, 14, 2 by shell.

Explain a configuration using the **energy** of the electrons and **inter-electron repulsion**. Electrons go to the lowest energy orbital available. Two electrons in one orbital repel more, so electrons occupy separate orbitals of equal energy first.
Sketch an s orbital as a sphere and a p orbital as a dumbbell with the nucleus at the centre.
Write the electrons-in-boxes for Fe as [Ar] [↑↓][↑][↑][↑][↑] for 3d, then [↑↓] for 4s.
For a **d-block ion**, the 4s electrons are lost first. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
Electrons occupy the lowest energy orbitals available, and repel each other.
In d-block ions the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons.
